questions.question: A 40-year-old Asian man presents to the Emergency Department with 4-day history of painful eye movements and deterioration of vision in both eyes. He reports having had a similar episode several years ago, which resolved after a course of treatment. Since he completed treatment, he now complains of lower limb weakness and sensory loss that is affecting his ability to walk. On examination, there is reduced visual acuity (6/30) in both eyes with evidence of colour desaturation during testing with Ishihara charts. There is 2/5 power in both lower limbs with reduced touch sensation and proprioception. An MRI of the patient's spine is requested and shows T2 enhancement of the cord with local swelling affecting T9, T10, T11 and T12. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Neuromyelitis optica

This patient has presented with symptoms of painful eye movements, colour desaturation and reduced visual acuity. This is in keeping with a diagnosis of optic neuritis. Additionally, he describes lower limb weakness and an MRI report shows enhancement of four vertebral levels, suggestive of transverse myelitis. The combination of these features is suggestive of a diagnosis of neuromyelitis optica (NMO) which is a rare, inflammatory and demyelinating disease characterised by bilateral optic neuritis and transverse myelitis affecting at least three vertebrae. The disease is more common in people of Asian and Afro-Caribbean backgrounds.

A. Lyme disease

Lyme disease is a rare cause of optic neuritis. The prodrome of the disease proceeds the onset of a tick bite followed by erythema migrans and neurological manifestations, including cranial nerve palsies and aseptic meningitis. This does not match the presentation of this patient.

B. Guillain-Barré syndrome

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is a demyelinating polyneuropathy associated with ascending paralysis, areflexia and sensory loss. Facial symptoms, including bulbar weakness, oropharyngeal weakness and ptosis may be present, but these are normally associated with trunk and upper limb involvement as the demyelination ascends. Additionally, the MRI report showing enhancement localised to T9-T12 nerve roots is more suggestive of transverse myelitis than GBS.

C. Multiple sclerosis

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a reasonable differential diagnosis given the presentation of optic neuritis, a classic association. However, bilateral optic neuritis is less common in MS compared with neuromyelitis optica (NMO).

Furthermore, transverse myelitis affecting over three vertebral levels is also more suggestive of NMO.

E. Systemic lupus erythematosus

Systemic lupus erythematosus is a chronic multisystem disorder that presents with various cardiovascular, renal, cutaneous and neurological symptoms. However, it is an uncommon cause of optic neuritis, particularly bilateral neuritis. Patients with this condition are also unlikely to present with transverse myelitis.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man has been admitted to the Coronary Care Unit late in the evening. Past medical history includes diabetes, glaucoma, hypertension, angina, transient ischaemic attacks and peripheral vascular disease. He had collapsed at home and, on arrival to hospital, was in complete heart block. After a few attempts, a transvenous pacing wire was inserted in the right internal jugular vein. During the night shift, the ward staff become concerned as his condition has deteriorated. He is complaining of a severe left frontal headache with associated nausea and vomiting. He also has blurring of vision in his left eye and has noted some flecks of bright red blood in his vomit. His temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 90/min regular, blood pressure 180/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min. Examination reveals a fixed dilated pupil on the left side. There is no other focal neurology. His abdomen is soft. What medication is likely to benefit this patient?
questions.explanation:
C. Acetazolamide

Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and has found use in the treatment of glaucoma and mountain sickness. This patient has been admitted with symptomatic complete heart block and would most likely have received atropine till the temporary pacing wire could be placed. Atropine is an anti-muscarinic drug, and in the eye it causes dilation of the pupil (mydriasis) and cycloplegia of the ciliary body. As a result it increases the risk of glaucoma with symptoms of localised frontal headache, blurring of vision, nausea and vomiting. The eye affected will classically have a fixed, dilated pupil with corneal oedema and peri-corneal ciliary injection. The treatment includes topical beta-blockers (timolol), which can be systemically absorbed, acetazolamide and topical pilocarpine. Acetazolamide can cause a normal anion gap acidosis. The patient will require measurement and monitoring of the intraocular pressure by an ophthalmologist.

D. Omeprazole

Omeprazole does not have a significant impact on acute glaucoma, the most likely diagnosis here.

A. Nitroprusside

Nitroprusside acts as a nitrate donor and is a vasodilator. As such, its main role is in the treatment of hypertension rather than acute glaucoma.

B. Labetalol

Although labetolol will achieve some exposure when given systemically to the eye, it may precipitate a worsening of heart block when given so soon after the transient episode.

E. Aspirin

Anti-platelet agents don't impact on acute glaucoma, and the patient is already likely to have been treated with an adequate dose of anti-platelet therapy.

questions.question: You are the Medical Registrar on call, and you are phoned by your Foundation (FY2) doctor who is covering the hospital at night. He is concerned about a 33-year-old woman who is currently an inpatient on the Gastroenterology Ward. He tells you that the nurses contacted him to review the patient after she complained of developing a red left eye. The patient was admitted into hospital 24 hours ago with a history of 2 weeks of severe abdominal pain accompanied by recurrent bouts of diarrhoea and blood-stained faeces. A colonoscopy was performed earlier in the day which showed numerous heterogeneous patches of inflammation. Your FY2 conveys that he has examined the patient, who is currently haemodynamically stable and well, but has a diffusely erythematous left eye, particularly in the lateral aspect, which feels 'gritty'. There is no evidence of an exudate. Of note, she can move the eye and her vision is unaffected. Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of her acute red eye?
questions.explanation:
D. Episcleritis

This patient likely has an underlying diagnosis of Ulcerative colitis (UC) for which she was admitted into hospital. Episcleritis is associated with a variety of inflammatory disorders, particularly UC and Crohn's Disease.

The hallmark of episcleritis is a mildly discomfort, gritty erythematous lesion of the eye, most commonly unilaterally, without discharge, watering or affecting acuity. Episcleritis is usually self-limiting.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Episcleritis.jpg This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International license.

A. Acute angle closure glaucoma

Acute angle closure glaucoma is an ophthalmological emergency. It is caused by a blockage of the drainage of the eye's aqueous humor. It is often associated with an impairment of vision. These patients often appear sick, with vomiting and nausea. It is characterised by increased intra-ocular pressure. Latanoprost is useful in the treatment of glaucoma. Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue which increases the aqueous outflow from the eye, and in so doing, reduces the intra-ocular pressure.

A topical beta blocker is another option. It works by reducing the volume of aqueous secretion. Importantly, topical beta blockers can be absorbed systemically and cause bradycardia.

B. Anterior uveitis

Uveitis, associated with disorders including Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is an inflammatory disease of the eye, which is often unilateral, is characterised by perilimbal injection (which is absent in this case) and a painful red eye which worsens over several hours. Vision is not usually impaired. The use of steroids is key in quickly reducing the inflammatory response seen in uveitis. Steroids may be given topically, orally, intravenously, intramuscularly or even by periocular injection. Steroid tapering must be performed slowly to prevent rebound inflammation. Topical administration can be as frequent as hourly in the beginning of treatment.

C. Conjunctivitis

Conjunctivitis is commonly associated with infection. It can present in the context of inflammatory disease but is characterised by the co-existence of discharge, which is absent in this case. Treatment of conjunctivitis is dependent on the cause. If a viral infection is suspected, treatment is usually supportive with simple advice including removal of contact lenses if present. If HSV is suspected, the use of a topic antiviral such as acyclovir is recommended. Similarly, bacterial conjunctivitis is most often self-limiting and usually does not require treatment.

E. Scleritis

Scleritis is commonly associated with inflammatory disorders, particularly rheumatoid arthritis (RA). It is characterised by severe pain which deteriorates on eye movement and may affect vision. Oral NSAIDs may be used in the treatment of scleritis and episcleritis. Episcleritis is usually a self-limiting illness. Scleritis, however which can be extremely painful and can also affect vision should be treated. Oral NSAIDs are generally recommended as first line treatment, typically oral ibuprofen four times daily. IF this does not improve symptoms, treatment can be switched to high dose steroids. 72224

questions.question: A 47-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with bilateral red eyes which are associated with feelings of pain and grittiness. There is no significant exudate from the eyes. His eyes are pictured below. This is the second time he has presented with eye problems over the past four months. On the previous occasion, the pain and redness settled with use of artificial tears. He has a history of inflammatory bowel disease which is currently managed with oral mesalazine. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
E. Topical corticosteroids

The sudden onset of bilateral red eyes in a patient with a history of inflammatory bowel disease is consistent with a diagnosis of episcleritis. Although the first episode responded to artificial tears, on this occasion, topical corticosteroids are a more appropriate intervention to control symptoms.

D. Topical chloramphenicol

A second episode of red eyes without significant exudate is more consistent with episcleritis, especially given the history of inflammatory bowel disease; hence, chloramphenicol is not of value in this patient.

A. Oral co-amoxiclav

Although this patient's eyes are red, there is no evidence of discharge, and the history of inflammatory bowel disease and recurrent eye symptoms drives us more towards a diagnosis of episcleritis.

B. Oral naproxen

Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are used for resistant episcleritis, although in this case, with a history of inflammatory bowel disease, topical therapy is the preferred option.

C. Oral prednisolone

Although systemic corticosteroids may be required for patients with resistant disease, in this case, a trial of topical corticosteroids is appropriate first.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman presents with sudden, painless loss of vision in her right eye. She describes blurred vision that progressed over a few hours. Her past medical history includes hypertension and diabetes. On examination, there is a relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye, and fundoscopic examination is as shown in the picture below. Visual acuity in the left eye is normal. What is the most appropriate initial investigation for diagnosing the cause of this patient's optic neuropathy?
options: A. MRI of the brain and orbits
questions.explanation:
A. MRI of the brain and orbits

The patient's fundoscopy shows optic disc swelling with surrounding haemorrhages. MRI of the brain and orbits is often the initial investigation of choice in cases of acute optic neuropathy with optic disc swelling, as it can help to identify inflammatory, ischaemic or compressive lesions affecting the optic nerve. This modality is essential to rule out possible structural or vascular causes and is especially relevant in cases with an afferent pupillary defect.

C. Optical coherence tomography

Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides a detailed view of retinal and optic nerve fibre layers and is helpful in evaluating optic neuropathy. However, while OCT can identify thinning in optic neuropathy, it is usually more useful in chronic cases or in monitoring progression rather than for acute diagnosis.

B. Temporal artery biopsy

Temporal artery biopsy is appropriate if giant cell arteritis is suspected, particularly in patients aged over 50 years presenting with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or elevated inflammatory marker levels. In this case, the absence of systemic symptoms and the patient's age suggest another cause for optic neuropathy, making temporal artery biopsy less appropriate as the initial investigation.

D. Visual evoked potentials

Visual evoked potentials is a functional test used to assess visual pathway integrity and is often used in demyelinating disease (such as multiple sclerosis). However, it is generally not the first-line investigation in acute optic neuropathy where imaging to exclude structural causes takes priority.

E. Fluorescein angiography

Fluorescein angiography is used to assess retinal vascular conditions and can detect ischaemic changes in the retina. It is not the primary investigation for optic neuropathy, as it provides limited information on the optic nerve itself, compared with MRI.

questions.question: A 63-year-old, known to have poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, presented to the ophthalmologist on-call complaining of floaters and decreased vision. The ophthalmologist has recommended that the patient has treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). There is evidence of macular oedema with extensive cotton wool spots, hard exudates and haemorrhages. Which of the following interventions is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
C. Ranibizumab

Ranibizumab is a recombinant humanised antibody fragment which is active against all forms of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-A. It has been shown in a number of clinical trials to be effective in improving visual acuity and reducing progression of proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

E. Triamcinolone

Intravitreal triamcinolone may be effective in relieving macular oedema in the short-term although, over the longer-term, it is associated with increased intra-ocular pressure.

A. Dexamethasone

Dexamethasone implants are used for patients with diabetic retinopathy who undergo cataract surgery, although steroid use in the general patient population may significantly increase intra-ocular pressure over time.

B. Infliximab

Infliximab is an anti-tumour necrosis factor (anti-TNF) antibody used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease and inflammatory arthritides. It is not used in the treatment of diabetic retinopathy.

D. Toclizumab

Toclizumab is an anti-IL6 monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.

A 45-year-old man, originally from Zimbabwe, attends the Emergency Department. He presents with abdominal pain which the Surgical Registrar has identified as acute appendicitis. While he is being prepared for theatre, the Surgical Registrar phones you as he is concerned that this man is visually impaired from an unknown cause. The patient is unable to speak English, but his General Practitioner (GP) records show that he attended his GP surgery two years ago. At the time, he was taking a course of Ivermectin, which he was given in Zimbabwe. His GP describes him as an otherwise well man. Clinical examination reveals patches of dry, thick, depigmented skin across the patient's face and torso. Investigations reveal the following:

Mid-stream urine (MCS) Negative

A chest X-ray reveals the following:

Which infective organism is most likely to be responsible for this patient's blindness?
questions.explanation:
D. Onchocerca Volvulus (O. Volvulus)

O. Volvulus is the most common cause of infective blindness worldwide and causes onchocerciasis, or river blindness. It enters the body after repeated bites from its host - the blackfly. It is endemic to many regions of Africa. It is associated with a significant inflammatory T cell mediated response and results in antigen deposition in tissue including the cornea. In addition, patients typically present with an itchy rash covering of large parts of their bodies.

A. Chlamidia Trachomatis (C. Trachomatis)

Trachoma is the second commonest cause of infective blindness worldwide. It is often transmitted from mother to child. It causes a follicular conjunctivitis which goes through several phases of inflammation which eventually causes fibrosis, scarring and corneal opacification. Antibiotics such as azithromycin can be used early to eradicate the infection, but occasionally, a surgical approach is required to prevent corneal scarring.

B. Mycobacterium Leprae (M. Leprae)

M. Leprae causes a granulomatous illness. It predominantly affects Schwann cells and can cause predominantly skin manifestations. Although this patient does have depigmented skin, there are no other features to suggest leprosy. Usually, the depigmented areas lack sensation. Worldwide, mycobacterium leprae is a common cause of peripheral neuropathy and can present with blindness secondary to neuropathy. Importantly, it can also cause direct inflammatory injury to the eye and corneal ulceration.

C. Mycobacterium Tuberculosis (TB)

The patient has no features of previous pulmonary or extra-pulmonary TB infection. Tuberculosis infection results in a macrophage response, which engulfs the organism. The bacteria remain active and a granuloma develops to "wall off" the infection. Gradually, the chronic inflammatory process results in systemic features of the disease including wasting, anorexia, low grade pyrexia and malaise. TB can affect other organs beside the lungs which occurs following spread into the bloodstream. Of note, in the gastrointestinal system, TB can result in ileocecal thickening. In the central nervous system, tuberculous meningitis can occur, and similarly, central nerves can become inflamed or injured. Tuberculous optic neuropathy is a rare complication.

E. Treponema Pallidum Pertenue

This bacterium is responsible for the infection known as Yaws, which is characterised by skin papillomas and ulceration. Neither of these major symptoms are described in this patient's presentation.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with sudden onset of eye pain, which is associated with loss of vision in the right eye. Her symptoms started when she was driving through a dark tunnel. She has no past history of ophthalmological problems. Her right pupil was fixed and dilated upon examination. Intraocular pressure was measured and found to be raised. Her eye inspection: Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the definitive treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
B. Peripheral iridotomy

This patient is presenting with acute eye pain after spending time in the darkness, as well as seeing visual halos. She also has impaired vision and a fixed and dilated pupil, all of which are concerning for acute angle- closure glaucoma. The definitive treatment for this condition is laser peripheral iridotomy, which involves creating a small hole in the iris with a laser to re-establish proper aqueous outflow.

Image source: Jonathan Trobe, M.D. (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acute_Angle_Closure- glaucoma.jpg), CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0), via Wikimedia Commons

C. Timolol drops

Timolol blocks beta-receptors to reduce aqueous humour production and is an appropriate initial medical treatment for angle-closure glaucoma. However, it is not the definitive therapy.

A. Intravenous (IV) acetazolamide

The history and examination findings in this patient indicate acute angle-closure glaucoma. The history of driving through a dark tunnel would seem to suggest that the attack was triggered by pupillary dilatation narrowing the iridocorneal angle.

IV acetazolamide is one of the treatment options for acute angle-closure glaucoma in the acute setting. Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with acute-onset eye pain, loss of peripheral vision and possible nausea and vomiting. IV acetazolamide is used in the acute setting but is not suitable for long-term prevention.

D. Topical pilocarpine

Pilocarpine acts as a muscarinic receptor agonist and causes miosis which opens the angle. However, this is not the definitive treatment for this condition.

E. Topical prostaglandin analogues

Topical prostaglandin analogues, such as latanoprost, tafluprost, travoprost and bimatoprost, are the first-line treatment for chronic open-angle glaucoma. They are not a definitive treatment for this patient's closed-angle glaucoma.

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a red right eye. She has a history of sarcoidosis. She is acutely photophobic and has her eyes closed. She tells you that her eye has become increasingly uncomfortable over a period of several hours. It became unbearable while she was driving. She managed to pull to the side of the road and contact an ambulance. On examination, her left eye appears normal. Comparatively, however, her right eye is grossly inflamed. Her vision is blurred. She can move her eye in all directions, and the redness appears most concentrated around the limbus of her right eye. She refuses to allow you to perform ophthalmoscopy. She is currently on no medication other than paracetamol as required. Previous medication includes Azathioprine which was weaned and ceased one year before this presentation. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to initiate for her acute red eye?
questions.explanation:
E. Topical steroids

The use of steroids is key in quickly reducing the inflammatory response seen in uveitis. Steroids may be given topically, orally, intravenously, intramuscularly, or even by periocular injection. Steroid tapering must be performed slowly to prevent rebound inflammation. Topical administration can be as frequent as hourly in the beginning of treatment.

A. Oral methotrexate

Oral methotrexate is a treatment option for uveitis and also scleritis, particularly because of its anti-metabolite properties which cause a downstream reduction in inflammation. Additionally, methotrexate is a recognised treatment for sarcoidosis and helps to reduce the severity of uveitis by also managing the underlying condition.

That being said, it is certainly not a first line treatment that should be started in this situation without careful planning and counselling.

B. Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

Oral NSAIDs may be used in the treatment of scleritis and episcleritis. Episcleritis is usually a self-limiting illness. Scleritis, however, can be extremely painful and can also affect vision. Oral NSAIDs are generally recommended as a first line treatment, typically in the form of oral ibuprofen four times a day. If this does not improve symptoms, treatment can be switched to high dose steroids.

C. Topical acyclovir

Red eye can be caused by either Herpes simplex virus (HSV) or Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. However, in this case, the patient was weaned off immune suppressing treatment and is less likely to contract these illnesses.

D. Topical latanoprost

Latanoprost is useful in the treatment of glaucoma. Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue which increases the aqueous outflow from the eye, and in so doing, reduces the intra-ocular pressure. There is no indication that this patient is suffering from glaucoma, so this would not be an appropriate treatment modality.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department (ED) complaining of a sudden loss of vision in his left eye. He describes the incident as 'something went black in one eye'. There is no pain or headache associated with his symptom. His past medical history is significant for atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Physical examination is normal, except for the presence of a carotid bruit. The findings on fundoscopic examination are shown in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)

This patient is presenting with sudden monocular vision loss, a cherry-red spot on the macula and a history of atrial fibrillation, suggesting a diagnosis of CRAO. Central retinal artery occlusion presents with sudden, painless vision loss in the affected eye. Fundoscopy will demonstrate a pale retina, a cherry-red spot at the fovea and oedema. This occurs because the loss of perfusion of the retina allows blood from the choroid to pass through. Risk factors include a hypercoagulable state and atrial fibrillation.

Image source: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Cherry_Red_Spot_Fiess.jpg - Achim Fieß, Ömer Cal, Stephan Kehrein, Sven Halstenberg, Inez Frisch, Ulrich Helmut Steinhorst, CC BY 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

E. Retinal detachment

Retinal detachment would present with vision loss typically described as 'a curtain coming down over the vision', with ultrasound showing a free flap in the eye.

B. Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)

In addition to loss of vision, CRVO classically presents with a 'blood and thunder appearance' due to extensive haemorrhages on fundoscopy.

C. Ischaemic stroke

Ischaemic stroke would present with focal neurological deficits that extend beyond just monocular vision loss.

Though this diagnosis is possible, the fundoscopy findings and an otherwise normal neurological examination go against this.

D. Migraine with aura

The fundoscopic image shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea and oedema, indicating CRAO.

In 'migraine with aura', patients suffer severe headaches, which may be associated with transient visual disturbance, generally lasting less than an hour, typically 10-30 minutes. Visual symptoms typically start before the headache ('aura') but may occur during the headache. They may consist of positive symptoms, negative symptoms or altered/distorted vision.

questions.question:
A 49-year-old man returns to the Endocrinology Clinic for a follow-up appointment. He has Graves' disease and is currently on a titration regimen, taking carbimazole 15 mg twice daily, with propranolol for symptom control. Over the last few weeks, he has been experiencing a gritty sensation in his eyes, although this has progressed to retro-orbital eye pain. He has double vision and reports that colours are less vivid and he has some blurring of his central vision. .
Thyroid Function TestResultNormal Value
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)0.15 mU/L0.4–5
Free thyroxine (FT4)19.7 pmol/L10–22
Free triiodothyronine (FT3)8.8 pmol/L5–10
What is the next most important treatment?
questions.explanation:
C. Methylprednisolone

This patient has thyroid eye disease secondary to Graves' disease. His condition is sight-threatening (note the blurred vision, diplopia and colour desaturation). Initial treatment in such cases is with IV glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone 500 mg once weekly and subsequent tapering regimen). If after 1-2 weeks, the response is poor or the treatment is poorly tolerated, then orbital decompression surgery would be recommended.

E. Radioiodine

Radioiodine is a definitive treatment option for Graves' thyrotoxicosis. There is a chance that it may aggravate thyroid eye disease and it is, therefore, not appropriate here.

A. Increase carbimazole

While the thyroid hormone levels indicate ongoing hyperthyroidism, the most urgent treatment here is for thyroid eye disease.

B. Naproxen

Non-steroidal analgesia can be useful for the pain of subacute thyroiditis and thyroid eye disease. However, it is not the most important treatment, given the threat to visual function.

D. Surgical decompression

Surgical orbital decompression may be required to save vision. However, this is usually performed for ongoing symptoms and signs after a course of glucocorticoids.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden painless loss of vision affecting the upper portion of vision out of her right eye. She suffered a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) at age 18 years but has no other significant past medical history. An image of her right retina is shown below. Her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, pulse is 88 bpm and regular, body mass index (BMI) is 24 kg/m². Which is the best investigation for the underlying cause of this event?
questions.explanation:
E. Thrombophilia screen

The symptoms of loss of the upper portion of the field of vision, coupled with a previous history of DVT in a young woman, raise the possibility of an inherited thrombophilia leading to BRVO. Hence, a thrombophilia screen to rule out anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, factor V Leiden mutation, protein C+S or antithrombin III deficiency is the most appropriate next step.

A. 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring

This patient's blood pressure is in the normal range despite significant anxiety, and we are given no indication of hypertension as a cause for branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO).

B. Fasting triglycerides

Although hypertriglyceridaemia is associated with BRVO, this is usually in the presence of very high triglyceride levels (up to 10 mmol/l); the absence of other features of hypertriglyceridaemia counts against this as the underlying cause.

C. HbA1c

Diabetes mellitus is a cause of thrombophilia but there is an absence of symptoms of hyperglycaemia here, and the BMI is in the normal range, making type 2 diabetes unlikely.

D. Immunoglobulin electrophoresis

Haematological malignancy including myeloma is a recognised cause of retinal vein occlusion, although the age here makes myeloma unlikely, and there are no associated symptoms of haematological malignancy.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner for a routine medical check-up. He has no specific complaints. His father died when he was young however, he is not sure of the details regarding the cause of his father's death. Childhood history is relevant for the presence of sore throat which was treated with appropriate antibiotics. On examination, his blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg and his heart rate is 80 bpm. The patient's eye is shown below: Which of the following findings is most likely to be present on physical examination?
options: A. A rough, rumbling mid-diastolic murmur in the left fifth ICS lateral to the mid-clavicular line
B. An ejection systolic murmur in the right second intercostal space (ICS)
questions.explanation:
C. Earlobe crease

This patient's family history and physical examination findings of corneal arcus suggest a diagnosis of familial hyperlipidaemia. It is associated with the presence of earlobe crease (Frank's sign), tendon xanthoma, eruptive xanthoma and xanthelasma.

Image Source: Afrodriguezg, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

E. Retinal degeneration

Retinal degeneration is seen in patients with disorders such as retinitis pigmentosa. Patients with familial hyperlipidaemia may have lipaemia retinalis on fundoscopic examination.

A. A rough, rumbling mid-diastolic murmur in the left fifth ICS lateral to the mid-clavicular line

These findings are suggestive of mitral stenosis. Although this patient gives a childhood history of sore throat, it was appropriately treated. Hence, it is unlikely that this patient has rheumatic heart disease.

B. An ejection systolic murmur in the right second intercostal space (ICS)

These findings are suggestive of aortic stenosis. However, this patient's age and absence of symptoms do not support the diagnosis of aortic stenosis. Early-onset aortic stenosis occurs in patients with bicuspid aortic valve and usually presents in the fifth decade.

D. Multiple scratch marks

Multiple scratch marks are seen in patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) due to the presence of severe pruritus. PBC is also associated with the presence of xanthelasma.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a severe headache, nausea and vomiting. He admits that he was diagnosed with hypertension some four years earlier but has refused to visit the general practitioner (GP) for follow-up. His brother has end-stage kidney disease. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg, and there are ballotable masses in both flanks. His body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m². A retinal photograph is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypertension?
questions.explanation:
D. Polycystic kidney disease (PKD)

The history of prolonged hypertension presenting now with grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy, coupled with signs of bilateral renal masses and end-stage kidney disease in his brother, fits with a diagnosis of autosomal dominant PKD. Although angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are the mainstay of therapy to control blood pressure in PKD, titratable intravenous (IV) therapy with nitroprusside or labetolol is likely to be more appropriate.

A. Adrenal carcinoma

Adrenal carcinoma is much more likely to be unilateral and is associated with features of Cushing syndrome and hyperandrogenism. The normal BMI and bilateral features count against Cushing syndrome as the cause of this patient's hypertension.

B. Cushing syndrome

Cushing syndrome may be associated with uncontrolled hypertension, although it is also associated with marked weight gain and dysglycaemia, which are not seen in this patient.

C. Phaeochromocytoma

Phaeochromocytoma may present with grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy, although the bilateral renal masses would not be seen in the context of an underlying phaeochromocytoma.

E. Reflux nephropathy

Reflux nephropathy does result in the development of hypertension, which may be severe, although it does not lead to bilateral renal masses.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman is referred by her General Practitioner with a 24-h history of gradual deterioration in her right visual acuity, associated with pain on eye movement, to the extent that she can now only perceive light. She also complains of a general feeling of fatigue for the past few weeks. She has no other neurological symptoms. There is nil to find on general examination but, fundoscopy of her right eye is shown below. What would be the most useful investigation to institute at this stage?
options: C. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan head
D. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)
questions.explanation:
C. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan head

The likely diagnosis here is optic neuritis (ON), which is a demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve, and although it is strongly associated with multiple sclerosis (MS), it can also occur on its own.

Decreased visual acuity secondary to optic neuritis may be permanent. Optic neuritis affects Caucasians more commonly than other races and there is a male : female ratio of 1 : 2. Symptoms include a rapid decline in visual acuity in one eye (rarely both) associated with pain exacerbated by eye movement and dyschromatopsia (change in colour perception).

Typically, patients with first-time acute ON are otherwise healthy young adults. In some cases, a history of preceding viral illness may be present. In acute ON, the optic disc may appear normal since two-thirds of cases of ON are retrobulbar. However, the optic nerve may become pale over time. In the remaining cases the optic disc can appear swollen, as here.

Patients with MS may have recurrent attacks of ON. Therefore, a history of previous episodes of decreased vision in the same or the fellow eye must be sought. A previous history of neurological problems, such as transient episodes of extremity/facial numbness, weakness or pins and needles, suggests a diagnosis of MS. A family history of MS may exist.

In a typical case of ON without any clinical signs and symptoms of a systemic disease, the yield from blood tests is low and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination is non-contributory to the diagnosis. MRI can be used to assess inflammatory changes in the optic nerves and helps exclude structural lesions.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Optic-neuritis-in-the-right-eye.jpg

D. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)

These are non-specific indicators of inflammation and may not be elevated in patients with multiple sclerosis.

A. Lumbar puncture

In a patient with unilateral papilloedema, imaging should be considered first before lumbar puncture is considered.

B. Computed tomography (CT) scan head

CT scanning, although useful in the acute situation to rule out a significant lesion, cannot achieve sufficient resolution to rule demyelination in or out as a potential diagnosis.

E. Visual evoked responses

These will confirm optic neuropathy, which is already suspected, although they will not contribute to determining the overall diagnosis. 70717

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with a history of primary open-angle glaucoma presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with sudden, painless loss of vision in his left eye. There is no history of flashes of light or floaters. His past medical history is significant for type II diabetes mellitus. Fundoscopic examination is performed and the findings are shown in the image attached. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most suitable treatment for this patient?
options: C. IV acetazolamide and ocular massage
D. Observation with elevation of head of the bed
questions.explanation:
C. IV acetazolamide and ocular massage

This patient has central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). There is currently no evidence-based treatment to reverse the visual loss in this ocular emergency. Several management options are employed. Among suggested treatments for this condition are: manual massage of the globe to dislodge the clot and administration of IV acetazolamide, along with decompression of the anterior chamber within the first hour of onset anterior chamber paracentesis various forms of thrombolysis.

Image source: sidthedoc, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

E. Offer ranibizumab

Ranibizumab is one of the treatments for retinal vein occlusion. It functions through anti-angiogenic properties.

Retinal vein occlusion can present in a similar way to arterial occlusion. However, a fundoscopy examination will help in making a differential diagnosis.

A. Cryotherapy

Cryotherapy is used as a treatment for retinal detachment which is characterised by photopsia and the 'curtain coming down over the eye' phenomenon.

B. Intravenous (IV) acetazolamide and pilocarpine

Intravenous acetazolamide and pilocarpine are used as treatments for acute angle-closure glaucoma. Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with eye pain, loss of peripheral vision and possible nausea and vomiting.

D. Observation with elevation of head of the bed

The fundoscopic image shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea and oedema, indicating CRAO.

Observation with elevation of the head of the bed at night-time is a conservative treatment for vitreous haemorrhage, which is characterised by sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye or with 'floaters'. Diabetic retinopathy is a major risk factor.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, controlled with twice-daily mixed insulin and metformin, comes to the clinic with worsening visual acuity over the past week. He admits to poor compliance with diet and use of insulin, and a recent HbA1c has been measured at 65 mmol/mol. His blood pressure is 149/88 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: E. Switch to basal bolus insulin therapy
questions.explanation:
B. Bevacizumab

This presence of hard exudates and haemorrhages within one disc diameter of the macula is suggestive of macular oedema. This fits with poor compliance and deteriorating visual acuity in a patient with type 2 diabetes and retinal changes within one disc diameter of the macula. Bevacizumab is an anti-VEGF agent which has been proven to reduce retinal thickness, oedema and reduce growth of new vessels and risk of bleeding. Focal laser therapy is the alternative.

A. Acetazolamide

Acetazolamide reduces intra-ocular pressure and has its main role in the treatment of acute glaucoma rather than diabetic macular oedema.

C. Dexamethasone implant

Although corticosteroids do reduce macular oedema over the short term, they are usually considered a second- line option to anti-VEGF or laser therapy.

D. Intravitreal triamcinolone

Corticosteroids are usually considered when laser or anti-VEGF therapy is unsuitable or ineffective in managing macular oedema.

E. Switch to basal bolus insulin therapy

In the short term, improved glycaemic control may actually worsen retinopathy rather than having a positive impact on eye disease, although over the longer term it will reduce progression. Definitive local therapy is usually considered first before intensifying insulin treatment.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset, painless loss of vision in her left eye - which occurred while lifting weights at the gym. She describes a 'curtain coming down' over her vision; she was subsequently unable to see through that eye. She has no jaw or shoulder pain. Clinical examination reveals a normal cardiovascular and respiratory assessments. A neurological assessment reveals changes in the appearance of her eyes, shown below. Blood tests are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her loss of vision?
questions.explanation:
B. Left-sided carotid artery dissection

This explains the presentation of an ischaemic left-sided amaurosis fugax and left-sided Horner's syndrome (evidenced by the miosis and ptosis of the left eye). An important cause of carotid artery dissection is vigorous physical exercise, which fits this patient's history of weightlifting.

Carotid artery dissection refers to the tearing of the intimal layer of the carotid artery. This results in the formation of a haematoma which compresses the vascular lumen and impairs blood supply. The commonest causes of dissection include idiopathic and trauma but can occur secondary to collagen disorders, including Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlo Syndrome. The vast majority of tears occur extracranially. Investigations include Doppler ultrasound (US), computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which can be performed with angiography. MRI has a high pick-up rate and is the preferred imaging modality. Treatment is aimed at preventing and managing stroke, and if appropriate, may include the use of antiplatelet and thrombolytic therapy in selected patients. Endovascular stenting of occlusion has been used safely to relieve the symptoms and prevent further ongoing ischaemia.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Miosis.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Miosis.jpg)

C. Pituitary adenoma

This does not explain the presentation of Horner's syndrome. The mass effect presents with compression of the optic chiasm and bitemporal hemianopia. Other ocular nerve palsies can occur. Mass effect results in the presentation of headaches, particularly the classic headache of raised intracranial pressure, which is worst on waking, coughing or lowering the head. Cerebral spinal-fluid (CSF) obstruction can occur, which may present with hydrocephalus. Pituitary adenomas, which originate from hormonal tissue can cause panhypopituitarism.

Surgical excision of pituitary tumours can be performed using a trans-sphenoidal approach.

A. Giant cell arteritis (GCA)

There is no history to support a diagnosis of GCA. The peak age of GCA is in the 60-80 year old age group. It is associated with an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Amaurosis fugax is a presenting feature but is also accompanied by jaw pain. Polymyalgia rheumatic often co-exists. The history is usually of an older patient who presents with the recent onset of a headache. The symptoms are usually accompanied by tenderness across the temporal and often mandibular and occipital regions of the head.

Given that this is an inflammatory illness, systemic symptoms are common and can include weight loss, malaise and anorexia. A temporal artery biopsy can be performed on the symptomatic side. Importantly, a negative biopsy does not exclude the diagnosis, given that its pathology includes skipping lesions. If claudication is present then this can be treated with up to 60 mg of prednisolone.

D. Right-sided carotid artery dissection

The signs and symptoms of carotid artery dissection are ipsilateral. In this case, the symptoms are confined to the left-hand side of the patient.

E. Subarachnoid haemorrhage

There is no history of headache. Classically, subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with a severe "thunderclap headache". While its absence does not make the diagnosis impossible, it is far less likely than the alternatives presented. Subarachnoid haemorrhage can arise secondary to the rupture of a cerebral aneurysm or secondary to trauma. It can present in a variety of ways, other than a headache. Importantly, bleeding vessels can result in raised intra-ocular pressure with secondary effects such as compression of vessels, causing stroke and compression of the brain parenchyma and coning through the foramen magnum. Arterial bleeding can also induce vasospasm and subsequent cerebral ischaemia.

Investigations include CT scans of the head, which can identify bleeding, and also help to assess the presence of raised intracranial pressure. A negative CT scan does not rule out the diagnosis, and a lumbar puncture should be performed if there is no raised intracranial pressure and high suspicion. A sample can be sent for assessment of xanthochromia, the breakdown products of red blood cells, which can aid the diagnosis.

Treatment goals of subarachnoid haemorrhage are to prevent ischaemia, coning and compression of brain parenchyma. This can be achieved by, firstly, intensive care unit (ICU) monitoring of patients, consideration of monitoring the intracranial pressure, and the use of permissive hypertension with close control. The administration of nimodipine can help to prevent vasospasm. Neurosurgical interventions can include emergency craniotomy and planned aneurysmal embolisation or clipping.

questions.question: A 77-year-old woman presents to the Clinical Pharmacology Clinic for review. Her general practitioner (GP) is concerned because he has noted the eye appearance shown below. She has no significant past medical history. Her blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg; her pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 24 kg/m². Her total cholesterol level is 4.5 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
D. Reassurance

This patient has arcus senilis, also known as corneal arcus, which may be indicative of significant hypercholesterolaemia. Although in this case of an elderly patient with normal blood pressure and normal total cholesterol level without a history of cardiovascular disease, there should be no need to institute lipid-lowering therapy.

B. Fenofibrate 160 mg

Most evidence for the use of fibrates comes from its use in mixed dyslipidaemia and in patients with hypertriglyceridaemia. Evidence in this population supports their effectiveness in reducing triglyceride levels, although evidence to support an impact on outcomes is mixed, particularly against a background of statin use.

A. Atorvastatin 10 mg

Given this patient's normal total cholesterol level and a lack of a previous cardiovascular history, statin therapy is not appropriate here.

C. Omega-3 supplement 1 g

Omega-3 supplements are of most use in patients with hypertriglyceridaemia and low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels. There is also evidence to support their use in secondary cardiovascular prevention.

Here they are of limited value.

E. Rosuvastatin 10 mg

Rosuvastatin is not indicated here with a cholesterol level in the normal range and no history of previous cardiovascular disease.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents to the Emergency Department. She has taken up badminton to lose weight and presents with sudden loss of the upper field of vision in her right eye during a game. On examination, the left eye shows evidence of hypertensive changes, the right reveals a swollen optic disc with retinal haemorrhages in all four quadrants, there is an afferent pupillary defect. Her blood pressure (BP) is 148/92 mmHg Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/l135 - 175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.5 × 10⁹/l4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/l
Platelets (PLT)199 × 10⁹/l150 - 400 × 10⁹/l
Sodium (Na+)140 mmol/l135 - 145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.9 mmol/l3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)130 μmol/l50 - 120 µmol/l
Cholesterol6.2 mmol/l< 5.2 mmol/l
HbA1c62.84mmol/mol < 48 mmol/mol [for diabetics]

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Central retinal vein occlusion

The correct answer is central retinal vein occlusion which occurs with increased frequency in patients with a history of diabetes mellitus. Both retinal haemorrhages and oedema of the optic disc, with an afferent pupil defect are typical of the condition. The area of visual field loss may be variable, particularly during the early stages after retinal vein thrombosis occurs. Colour Doppler imaging is a non-invasive way to image the retrobulbar circulation, but the investigation of choice is fluorscein angiography. Blood work is targeted at identifying any underlying cause of hypercoagulability and consideration of either anti-platelet agents such as aspirin or anti-coagulation with warfarin. No effective treatments for central retinal vein occlusion have been identified although intra-ocular corticosteroids may have a role to play in associated macular oedema. Ischaemic optic neuropathy usually presents with a pale white oedematous optic disc.

A. Optic neuritis

Optic neuritis is incorrect because it does not cause flame haemorrhages in all four quadrants.

B. Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy

Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is incorrect because ischaemic optic neuropathy usually presents with a pale white oedematous optic disc.

C. Branch retinal vein occlusion

Branch retinal vein occlusion is incorrect because it causes sectoral haemorrhages, and not haemorrhages in all four corners which is more likely to be caused by a central retinal vein occlusion.

E. Central retinal artery occlusion

Central retinal artery occlusion is incorrect because it causes a pale fundus with a cherry class red spot at the macula, rather than with flame haemorrhages in all four quadrants of the eye, like in this scenario.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old housewife attends the Diabetic Clinic for her annual review. She has been an insulin-dependent diabetic for eight years and her blood sugar level is usually between 5 and 9 mmol/l. She leads a sedentary lifestyle, is obese and smokes about 10 cigarettes/day. On examination, her blood pressure is 140/95 mmHg and her pulse is 68 bpm and regular. Blood results:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)134 g/l135 - 175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.2 × 10⁹/l4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/l
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)78fl 80 - 100 fl
Platelets (PLT)214 × 10⁹/l150 - 400 × 10⁹/l
Hb A 1c85mmol/mol < 42 mmol/mol
Sodium (Na+)135 mmol/l135 - 145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.0 mmol/l3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l
Urea7.3 mmol/l2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)131 mmol/l50 - 120 µmol/l
24-hour urine protein30mg < 0.2g
Fundoscopy Normal

How often would you screen this patient for retinopathy?
options: D. No need for screening for the next five years
E. Screening only when she has visual symptoms
questions.explanation:
C. Annually

All people with type I and type II diabetes are offered annual retinal screening under the NHS Diabetic Retinopathy screening program. Those patients with diabetic retinopathy are followed up more frequently via the Ophthalmology Service.

A. Every two years

Every two years is incorrect. All people with type I and type II diabetes are offered annual retinal screening under the NHS Diabetic Retinopathy screening program.

B. Every six months

Every six months is incorrect. In the first instance, screening should be offered annually. If the patient is then found to have retinopathy, the Opthalmology Department may choose to review her more frequently.

D. No need for screening for the next five years

No need for screening for the next five years is incorrect because it does not follow the guidelines of the National Diabetic Retinopathy Screening program - it is recommended that diabetics are screened at least annually for retinopathy.

E. Screening only when she has visual symptoms

Screening only when she has visual symptoms is incorrect. All people with type I and type II diabetes are offered annual retinal screening under the NHS Diabetic Retinopathy screening program, regardless of their visual status/symptoms.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with reduced vision in the right eye noticed while taking a photograph. On examination, he has a right afferent pupillary defect and the following appearance on fundoscopy: Which one of the following should be undertaken soon?
questions.explanation:
A. Blood pressure measurement

The slide shows a fundus with grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy with optic disc oedema, cotton-wool spots and widespread A-V nipping. The retina looks oedematous. The other features one may see are flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages and hard exudate; which may collect around the fovea producing a 'macula star'. The presence of end-organ damage like this dictates the urgency with which this condition is managed. Obviously, the blood pressure needs to be recorded and optimally controlled. The diagnosis of hypertensive retinopathy is made by the presence of these retinal features in association with severely raised blood pressure.

Considering the other consequences of hypertension the following ought also to be done: urinalysis, CXR, and ECG +/- echo to look for renal damage and LVH/strain respectively. More broadly one must consider not only the consequences of the hypertension but also its causes, such as renal or endocrine disease.

E. Carotid Doppler

The presence of a carotid bruit does not dictate the need to do an urgent carotid doppler ultrasound.

B. Thyroid function

This is not the appearance chorioretinitis which may be caused by Toxoplasma, or dysthyroid eye disease. The latter can cause optic atrophy from optic nerve compression if there is increased pressure in the orbit.

C. Chest X-ray

A CXR needs to be done but not at the expense of everything else here.

D. Referral for fluorescein angiography

Fluorescein angiography is not required to make the diagnosis.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Ophthalmologist with decreased peripheral vision that is more pronounced at night for the past 12 months. She has no significant past medical or family history. On examination, visual acuity is found to be 6/12 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye. There is no restriction of extraocular movements. Bilateral pupils are equal and reacting to light. Colour vision is normal. The fundus picture is shown below: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Retinitis pigmentosa

Retinitis pigmentosa presents with night blindness and progressive visual field constriction with preserved central acuity until advanced disease. Fundoscopic appearances include the classic triad of attenuation of retinal blood vessels, waxy pale appearance of the optic disc and retinal pigmentation in a bone-spicule pattern.

Retinitis pigmentosa comprises of a group of dystrophies with around 70% of patients having a positive family history, although there are variable inheritance patterns. There is no cure for retinitis pigmentosa.

Image Source: Christian Hamel, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons

A. Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy would usually present with acute reduced visual acuity or an episode of amaurosis fugax, rather than the progressive symptoms seen here. The presence of bony spicules in the peripheral retina is also more suggestive of retinitis pigmentosa.

B. Chronic open angle glaucoma

Chronic open angle glaucoma causes peripheral contraction of the visual field and does not cause a decrease in night vision. The fundus picture is not suggestive of chronic open angle glaucoma.

C. Dry macular degeneration

Macular degeneration causes loss of central vision and colour perception is gradually lost. These are not features seen in this patient.

E. Vitamin A deficiency

Although vitamin A deficiency can cause night blindness, the presence of bony spicules in the peripheral retina is more suggestive of retinitis pigmentosa.

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Eye Clinic, following a referral from the optometrist. She presented with difficulty with the centre of her vision and at night. She tells you that her father progressively lost sight until he went blind at the age of 46. General physical examination is unremarkable. A picture of her left retina is shown below. The right retina has similar changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation:
D. Genetic testing

The scenario here showing deteriorating visual acuity in an 18-year-old with extensive drusen and a history of blindness in the family fits with an autosomal dominant condition. The most likely diagnosis is malattia leventinese, an autosomal dominant cause of blindness which results in a deterioration of the Bruch's membrane. A mutation which causes the disease has been mapped to chromosome 2.

C. Folic acid levels

Like vitamin B 12 deficiency, folate deficiency results in the development of optic neuropathy, which is reversible on the introduction of folic acid replacement.

A. Vitamin B 12 levels

Vitamin B 12 deficiency results in optic neuropathy, with optic disc pallor and loss of visual acuity, rather than the picture seen here with extensive drusen.

B. Fasting blood glucose

Features of diabetic retinopathy include haemorrhages, hard exudates and cotton-wool spots, rather than the picture seen here with drusen.

E. Vitamin A levels

Drusen are a feature of age-related macular degeneration, which may be positively impacted upon by vitamin A supplementation. However, the evidence here is for an autosomal dominant disorder such as malattia leventinese.

questions.question: You review a 52-year-old farmer who rarely consults with medical services. He complains of ocular pain and loss of vision. High magnification slit lamp examination reveals neovascular tufts of capillaries at the pupillary margin. The pupil is poorly reactive. Retinal photography reveals bilateral cotton wool spots, hard exudates, aneurysms and small dot-and-blot haemorrhages. He has a past history of diabetes and hypothyroidism. You suspect rubeosis iridis and subsequent glaucoma. His blood pressure is 135/82 mmHg. The most recent HbA1c is measured at 61 mmol/mol, and his TSH is 2.5. Which of the following is the most important preventative intervention to reduce the risk of glaucoma in this patient?
options: A. Tighter control of blood pressure
B. Tighter control of blood glucose
questions.explanation:
D. Pan-retinal photocoagulation

An important part of the work-up of rubeosis iridis is with fluorescein angiography to assess the extent of retinal ischaemia, and ultrasound. Once eye disease has progressed to rubeosis, the mainstay of therapy is pan- retinal photocoagulation to reduce the area of viable retina. Anti-VEGF agents and topical steroids may also be of value, but ultimately the prognosis is poor because of late stage at presentation.

E. Oral acetazolamide

This is a potential intervention for acute glaucoma.

A. Tighter control of blood pressure

There is limited scope to further improve blood pressure control here, and the patient already has advanced retinal disease, meaning any impact of improved blood pressure control on disease progression will be limited.

B. Tighter control of blood glucose

HbA1c, like blood pressure, is only slightly above target, hence any impact of tightening of blood glucose control on disease progression will be limited.

C. Increased thyroxine dose

TSH is in the normal range, meaning there is gain to be had from increasing thyroxine.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with severe right eye pain for the last three hours. Her eye pain is associated with headaches and blurring of vision, which she describes as coloured halos. Her left eye is unaffected. Her past medical history is significant for hypertension and psoriatic arthritis. Her medications include methotrexate and ramipril. On inspection, her eye is red. Further ophthalmology examination reveals the right pupil to be mid-dilated and less reactive to light, as compared to the left eye. Intraocular pressure is measured as 44 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Acute angle closure glaucoma

This patient has acute angle-closure glaucoma, which occurs when the natural drainage system for aqueous outflow is obstructed. The angle refers to the area between the iris and the cornea, through which fluid must flow to escape via the trabecular meshwork. When this angle is closed, intraocular pressure rises rapidly (as in this case), causing compression of the vessels that oxygenate. Patients usually present with ocular pain, a red eye, elevated intraocular pressures, decreased vision and a fixed, dilated pupil.

Image source: Jonathan Trobe, M.D., CC BY 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

B. Allergic conjunctivitis

The image shows a right eye with a hazy cornea and marked conjunctival injection.

Allergic conjunctivitis is a non-infectious form of conjunctivitis and is due to a reaction to an allergen in contact with the surface of the eye. Conjunctivitis is a diagnosis of exclusion. All forms of conjunctivitis can involve redness and discharge in one or both eyes and adhesion of the upper and lower eyelids on waking. Vision can appear blurred at times, but true visual acuity is normal. Conjunctivitis is not usually painful unless complicated by keratitis. Conjunctivitis is typically bilateral and does not raise intraocular pressure. All these are factors that point to a different diagnosis.

C. Cluster headache

Cluster headaches are one of the most painful types of headaches. In cluster headaches, patients commonly wake up in the middle of the night with intense pain around one eye and on one side of the head. Attacks can occur over the course of weeks to months, usually followed by remission periods when the headaches stop. The history of this patient makes a different diagnosis more likely.

D. Drug-induced glaucoma

Drug-induced glaucoma should be considered if there is a history of medications causing glaucoma such as steroids. This is a form of secondary glaucoma because it is brought about by specific systemic or topical medications.

E. Migraine headache

A migraine typically consists of a headache that often comes with nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light. It can last hours or days. While unilateral headache would fit with migraine, the presentation with red eye and raised intraocular pressure points to a different diagnosis.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man who works in a boarding kennels for cats and dogs is referred by his general practitioner (GP) after he presented complaining of right ocular pain and blurred, 'hazy' vision for several weeks. The fundal appearance is shown below: What is the most likely cause of this appearance?
questions.explanation:
A. Toxoplasmosis

The image shows chorioretinitis with vitritis, hence obscuring the optic disc, caused by Toxoplasma gondii infection. The symptoms associated with ocular toxoplasmosis include unilateral, mild ocular pain, blurred vision and new onset of floating spots. Patients often describe their vision as hazy. Clinical findings may include granulomatous iritis, optic disc swelling, neuroretinitis, vasculitis and retinal vein occlusion in the vicinity of the inflammation in the actively involved eye.

Fundoscopically, active toxoplasmosis presents with white-yellow chorioretinal lesions and vitreous cells.

There may be old, inactive lesions in the other eye. Congenital reactivation of toxoplasmosis accounts for the majority of cases encountered in clinical practice. Infection may also occur from ingestion of contaminated or undercooked meat and dairy products and direct or indirect ingestion of cat faeces.

Treatment is with at least four weeks of pyrimethamine/sulphadiazine/folinic acid clindamycin/sulphadiazine/atovaquone. Weekly full blood count would be required.

D. Cytomegalovirus

The fundal changes are inconsistent; Cytomegalovirus causes haemorrhagic retinitis. Furthermore, patients are usually immunosuppressed or suffer from a chronic illness such as HIV.

B. Retinitis pigmentosa

This is a chronic genetic retinal degeneration that does not cause pain and vitritis. Blindness is slowly progressive over a number of years. Peripheral visual field loss occurs first and is slowly progressive.

C. Retrobulbar neuritis

The man has no fundal signs and it is often a presenting feature of multiple sclerosis, for which other signs or symptoms are absent.

E. Retinal detachment

This usually occurs against a background of eye disease such as that related to diabetes mellitus. The area of detachment may be visualised on fundoscopy, including any area of retinal haemorrhage.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a fracture which he sustained while playing football. He is accompanied by his friends who explain that he fell while playing and broke his arm. Clinical examination reveals a young man who appears to have learning disabilities. He is tall and very thin. He appears to be scoliotic, and the radiograph of his arm demonstrates multiple acute radial fractures and decreased bone density. You organise for him to be reviewed by the Ophthalmology team on a subsequent follow-up assessment, who report a downward dislocation of the lens of his right eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Homocysteinuria

Homocysteinuria follows an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance and is characterised by impaired metabolism of methionine, an amino acid, caused by a deficiency in the enzyme cystathionine beta synthetase.

Classically, homocysteinuria presents with a marfanoid body habitus and a kyphoscoliotic spine. These patients are also characterised by learning disabilities and a downward dislocation of the lens. Of note, cardiac abnormalities are rare in this group of patients compared to the frequency noted in Marfans.

E. Marfans syndrome

This patient has presented with learning disabilities and osteoporosis. These features are less frequently seen in people with Marfans. Additionally, the dislocation of the lens in Marfans is upwards, rather than downwards, as seen in this patient's presentation.

A. Cystinosis

Cystinosis is a rare, inherited disorder characterised by renal abnormalities, particularly Fanconi Syndrome.

Cystinosis is a genetic disorder, which is inherited via an autosomal recessive pattern. It is a lysosomal storage disorder which results in the accumulation of cysteine. As cystine accumulates, it becomes deposited in a variety of tissues, including the eye, pancreas and kidneys, but can generally accumulate anywhere in the body, including muscle, brain and liver. Treatment is targeted at the removal of cystine, by cystine-depleting therapy and adequate hydration. Ultimately, however, renal progression in cystinosis is largely irreversible and is treated with renal replacement therapy and transplantation.

B. Cystinuria

This is a rare inherited stone-forming disease of the kidneys. Cystinuria is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern and results in a loss of renal reabsorption of the amino acid cystine (hence cystinuria), among other amino acids. Consequently, cystine-based stones forms along the urinary tract where cystine crystallises, particularly in acidic urine. Diagnosis is dependent on radiological imaging of the urinary tract, by computed tomography (CT), which confirms the presence of stones. Urinary cystine can be measured which, along with a good history, including a family history can make the diagnosis. Treatments involves urinary alkalinisation, which can be achieved with the use of citrate supplementation.

C. Ehlers Danlos (ED)

ED is an inherited disorder of joint hypermobility. There are a variety of subtypes of ED with varying genetic modes of inheritance. The classic form of the disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

Pathologically, type V collagen formation is affected with consequential hyperextensibility of skin, skin fragility, easy bruising and hypermobile joints. Lens abnormalities do not characterise it. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy form the backbone of managing this illness.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with complaints of seeing 'moving bubbles' in her left eye. Her symptoms have been worse for the last two weeks. She has noted no associated pain, photophobia or headache. Her past medical history is significant for hypertension, for which she takes lisinopril. On examination, her visual acuity is found to be 6/18 in the right eye and 6/60 in the left eye. Pupils are equal and reactive to light. No extraocular muscle deficit is noted. Fundoscopic examination: What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: C. Multivitamins, zinc and other antioxidants
E. Offer anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) medication
questions.explanation:
C. Multivitamins, zinc and other antioxidants

This patient is presenting with visual distortion, bilateral decrease in vision and a fundoscopic examination positive for 'drusen', suggesting the diagnosis of dry age-related macular degeneration (ARMD). The recommended initial therapy is multivitamin and antioxidant supplements.

Image source: Ipoliker, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

D. Observe the patient

No definitive treatment is indicated for retinal vein occlusion. Retinal vein occlusion presents as sudden, painless monocular vision loss. Fundoscopic examination would show retinal haemorrhage and venous dilatation.

A. Acetazolamide drops

Acetazolamide drops are used to treat open-angle glaucoma by decreasing aqueous humour production. Open- angle glaucoma presents as painless peripheral vision loss, resulting in 'tunnel vision'. Optic disc atrophy can be seen on fundoscopy.

B. Hyperbaric oxygen

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be beneficial in patients with central retinal artery occlusion, characterised by acute painless monocular vision loss. Fundoscopic examination would show a pale retina with attenuated vessels and a 'cherry-red' macula.

E. Offer anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) medication

Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is a signalling protein that stimulates the formation of blood vessels.

Anti-VEGF (antibodies directed at VEGF) can be used to treat wet ARMD. Anti-VEGF is also used in the treatment of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Both wet ARMD and proliferative diabetic retinopathy will show forms of neovascularisation on fundoscopic examination. This patient's fundoscopic image shows numerous large drusens, with no neovascularisation, hence indicating dry ARMD.

questions.question: A 76-year-old Asian woman presents to the Emergency Department. She complains of sudden-onset headache that began on leaving the cinema. She further describes altered vision and intractable vomiting. Examination is difficult as she is so agitated; however, digital palpation of the globe through closed eyelids reveals a rock-hard eyeball. Positive findings are pallor and sweating and she has a fixed dilated right pupil with lacrimation and injected conjunctiva. Fundoscopy is impossible. What is the optimal initial management?
questions.explanation:
A. Intravenous acetazolamide

This patient presents with acute angle closure glaucoma. This is caused by a sudden rise in intraocular pressure secondary to impaired flow of aqueous humour triggered in dim light when the pupil dilates. This condition often presents to physicians and can be misdiagnosed because of associated headache and abdominal pain.

Physical examination reveals decreased acuity, conjunctival injection and a fixed mid-position pupil, often oval in shape. Immediate treatment is necessary to preserve vision. Urgent ophthalmology referral is required. While waiting for specialist input, the carbonic-anhydrase inhibitor acetazolamide may be given to decrease aqueous humour production under ophthalmology instruction.

E. High-flow oxygen

High-flow oxygen is the intervention of choice for patients suffering from cluster headache.

B. Subcutaneous sumatriptan

Sumatriptan is an intervention of choice for acute migraine; although migraine may present with frontal headache, the rock-hard eye ball effectively rules it out as the underlying diagnosis here.

C. Intravenous dexamethasone

Topical prednisolone, not intravenous dexamethasone, is the usual intervention in patients with acute angle closure glaucoma.

D. Oral indomethacin

Indomethacin is the drug of choice for treating paroxysmal hemicrania, which is excluded here by the condition of the eye itself.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department (ED) describing a sudden onset of severe pain in his right eye, which occurred while he was at home, watching television. He is a student and has no medical conditions of note; he takes no medication and no illicit drugs. He tells you that this is the first time he has experienced eye pain like this. He rarely suffers from headache and has had no trauma. On examination, he has a normal-appearing cornea with an oval pupil. There is no visible discharge from the eye. There is no significant pain on eye movement, and the eye is not tender. He refuses further examination of his eye. His eye is seen below: Further history reveals a history of back pain which usually diminishes on his walk to and from University. He has no other history of joint aches, rash, dry mouth, or gastrointestinal symptoms. He does, however, complain of severe pain under his heels bilaterally which is worst, first thing in the morning and often dissipates while walking and with a massage. His General Practitoner (GP) has given him oral ibuprofen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Anterior Uveitis

A young man with a history of lower back pain which eases on physical activity should raise suspicions of an underlying Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS). AS is a multi-system inflammatory arthropathy which presents classically in young men and is characterised by deforming inflammatory arthritis of the vertebral column. Iritis, or anterior uveitis, is an important presenting feature of AS. It is characterised by an acutely painful red eye with photophobia. Uveitis can also be seen in Behçet syndrome. Further examination of the eye shows perilimbal injection. A hypopyon may be present, which is associated with Human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) related illnesses.

Image source: By Jonathan Trobe, M.D, CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?

curid=25691221

D. Optic Neuritis

Optic neuritis refers to a diagnostic made upon examination of the retina and optic nerve of a patient with visual disturbance. It is characterised by painful eye movements and the appearance of a swollen, inflamed optic nerve. It does not present with an acute red eye. It is associated with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.

B. Conjunctivitis

Conjunctivitis is a common presentation of red-eye. It does not, however, usually present without concurrent grittiness or discharge of the eye and is usually not associated with photophobia.

C. Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca

Keratoconjunctivitis sicca refers to a progressive illness of the cornea and conjunctiva, which is characterised by persistent dryness. It is most commonly associated with Sjogren syndrome. In this patient's presentation, there is no indication of dryness.

E. Scleritis

Scleritis refers to inflammation of the sclera of the eye. Importantly, scleritis can be associated with connective tissue disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis. It tends to present with a deep boring type pain of the eye which is often painful on movement and is tender.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus has been referred to the Diabetic Clinic by her general practitioner (GP) for difficulty in reading small print. This visual problem had gradually developed over several months. She has been diabetic for 11 years and has been controlled by diet alone. The patient is obese and smokes 15 cigarettes a day. She has a past medical history of hypertension and hyperlipidaemia and takes atenolol 50 mg od. On examination, her blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg and her pulse was 66 bpm and regular. Fundoscopy reveals non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR). Her FBC and U/Es are normal. Her HbA1c was 63.93 mmol/mol (8.0%). What is the most likely outcome of replacing diet by drug treatment in this patient?
options: A. Intensive blood glucose control would significantly decrease the risk of macrovascular disease
B. Intensive blood glucose control would lead to a reduction in the progression of retinopathy and deterioration of visual acuity
C. Intensive blood glucose control would reverse the progression of the retinopathy and improve her vision
D. Metformin would increase fasting plasma insulin
E. Metformin would be associated with less weight gain but with frequent hypoglycaemic episodes
questions.explanation:
B Intensive blood glucose control would lead to a reduction in the progression of retinopathy and deterioration of visual acuity The United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) was designed to establish whether intensive blood glucose control was of benefit in reducing the microvascular and macrovascular complications of type II diabetes. It also studied the outcome with different treatments. Diabetic control was assessed by measurements of HbA1c and was found to be significantly better in drug treatment groups than those treated by diet alone.
